summary: Where each endocrine gland comes from in the embryo: the thyroid from the floor of the pharynx, the parathyroids and C cells from the pharyngeal pouches, the pituitary from two ectoderm sources, the adrenal from mesoderm plus neural crest, and the islets from foregut endoderm. Exam questions tie each origin to the defect, ectopic tissue, or tumor that results.

points: The thyroid is the first endocrine gland to form, starting around week 4 as an endodermal diverticulum in the floor of the pharynx.
Its origin is marked in the adult by the foramen cecum, a pit at the junction of the anterior two thirds and posterior third of the tongue.
The gland descends in the midline, anterior to the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages, and stays linked to the tongue by the thyroglossal duct.
It reaches its final place in front of the trachea by about week 7, and the duct normally disappears.
A leftover duct segment can form a thyroglossal duct cyst: a midline neck mass that rises when the tongue is protruded.
A lower remnant of the duct can persist as a pyramidal lobe.
Failed descent leaves a lingual thyroid at the base of the tongue, which may be the patient's only thyroid tissue.
notes.why: The thyroid begins as an endodermal outpouching at the foramen cecum and is drawn down the front of the neck as the tongue and pharynx grow, trailing the thyroglossal duct behind it. Anything that stops this descent or fails to obliterate the duct leaves thyroid tissue or epithelium somewhere along that midline track. A duct cyst stays tethered to the tongue base through the duct remnant, which is why it rises when the tongue is protruded. A lingual thyroid may be the only functioning thyroid tissue, so removing it without imaging first can leave the patient hypothyroid.

points: Third pouch: dorsal wing forms the inferior parathyroids, ventral wing forms the thymus.
Fourth pouch: forms the superior parathyroids.
The inferior parathyroids travel down with the thymus, so they end up below the superior pair and can stop anywhere along that path, including in the thymus or anterior mediastinum.
The ultimobranchial body (from the caudal part of the fourth pouch) joins the thyroid and carries in neural crest cells that become parafollicular C cells (calcitonin).
notes.why: Each gland's adult position reflects how far its pouch tissue migrates. Third pouch tissue travels with the thymus toward the chest, so the inferior parathyroids end up lower than the fourth pouch superior parathyroids even though they start higher, and ectopic inferior glands sit in the thymus or mediastinum. C cells reach the thyroid from neural crest by way of the ultimobranchial body, which is why medullary thyroid carcinoma is a calcitonin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor unrelated to follicular cell cancers.

points: Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis): Rathke pouch, an upgrowth of oral ectoderm from the roof of the stomodeum.
Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis): the infundibulum, a downgrowth of neuroectoderm from the floor of the diencephalon.
The two parts meet and Rathke pouch loses its connection to the mouth.

Remnants of Rathke pouch can give rise to craniopharyngioma: a calcified, cystic suprasellar mass, common in children (with a second peak in older adults), that can cause bitemporal hemianopia and hypopituitarism.
notes.why: The pituitary is a composite gland: the anterior lobe is glandular epithelium from the roof of the mouth, and the posterior lobe is an extension of the brain. This origin explains its control: the anterior lobe answers to blood-borne releasing hormones carried by a portal system, while the posterior lobe releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons from their axon terminals. Craniopharyngioma grows from epithelial rests of Rathke pouch above the sella, so it presses on the optic chiasm, stalk, and hypothalamus, causing visual field loss, hypopituitarism, and sometimes diabetes insipidus.

points: Cortex: mesoderm (coelomic epithelium of the posterior abdominal wall), first as a large fetal cortex, then the adult cortex.
Medulla: neural crest cells that invade the cortex and become chromaffin cells, which act like postganglionic sympathetic neurons.
Neural crest tumors of the medulla: pheochromocytoma (mainly adults, episodic catecholamine excess) and neuroblastoma (children, the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood).
notes.why: The cortex and medulla have separate origins, so they behave as two glands inside one capsule. The mesodermal cortex makes steroids from cholesterol, while the neural crest medulla is in effect a sympathetic ganglion whose cells release catecholamines into blood when stimulated by preganglionic cholinergic fibers. Because neural crest cells also populate the sympathetic chain, neuroblastoma and paraganglioma can arise outside the adrenal anywhere along that chain.

points: The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail to develop normally.
Absent or small parathyroids, so little PTH: neonatal hypocalcemia with tetany or seizures.
Absent or small thymus: T cell deficiency, recurrent viral and fungal infections, and no thymic shadow on chest X-ray.
Also conotruncal heart defects (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot), cleft palate, and abnormal facies.
notes.why: A microdeletion at 22q11.2 (including the TBX1 gene) disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and of the neural crest cells that populate the pharyngeal arches and cardiac outflow tract. Each feature traces to one of these structures: parathyroids and thymus come from the pouches, and neural crest builds the conotruncal septum that divides the outflow tract. Hypocalcemia follows directly from absent PTH, and the T cell deficit follows from absent thymic maturation, while B cell numbers are typically normal.

points: The pancreas forms from dorsal and ventral buds of foregut endoderm.
The ventral bud forms the uncinate process and part of the head; the dorsal bud forms the rest.
Islet cells arise from the same endoderm as the ducts and acini, appear around the third month, and begin secreting insulin around the fifth month.
notes.why: Islet cells differentiate from the same foregut endodermal progenitors as ducts and acini, under transcription factors such as PDX1, so the endocrine and exocrine pancreas share one origin. Fetal insulin acts as a fetal growth factor. Maternal hyperglycemia crosses the placenta and drives fetal beta cell hyperplasia, which explains macrosomia and the neonatal hypoglycemia that follows when the maternal glucose supply stops at birth.

tricks.text: The third pouch gives the inferior parathyroids and the fourth gives the superior ones. The third pouch glands ride down with the thymus, so they pass the fourth pouch glands on the way.

tricks.text: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia from absent parathyroids, all from a deletion on chromosome 22 (22q11.2).

tricks.label: Mouth up, brain down
tricks.text: The anterior pituitary grows up from the roof of the mouth (Rathke pouch) and the posterior pituitary grows down from the brain (infundibulum).

highYield: A midline neck mass that moves up when the tongue sticks out is a thyroglossal duct cyst; a lateral mass along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid points to a branchial cleft cyst.
Check for normal thyroid tissue in the neck before removing a lingual thyroid, since it may be the only functioning thyroid.
Hypocalcemic tetany in the first days of life with absent thymic shadow means DiGeorge syndrome.
A missing inferior parathyroid adenoma at neck surgery is often found in the thymus or anterior mediastinum.
Craniopharyngioma is the classic calcified suprasellar mass in a child and comes from Rathke pouch.
Both pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma make catecholamines because both come from the neural crest sympathoadrenal lineage.
pitfalls: The inferior parathyroids come from the third pouch and the superior ones from the fourth; the numbers run opposite to adult position.
C cells sit in the thyroid but come from neural crest, while follicular cells come from endoderm.
The adrenal cortex is mesoderm and the medulla is neural crest; only the medulla gives neuroblastoma and pheochromocytoma.
Posterior pituitary tissue is neural tissue that stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus.

summary: What each endocrine gland looks like under the microscope, which cell makes which hormone, and which germ layer each cell type comes from. Exam questions show a slide description and ask for the hormone, the disease, or the stain that fits.

points: Follicles: a single layer of follicular cells surrounding colloid, which is stored thyroglobulin.
Resting gland: flat to cuboidal cells and large follicles full of colloid.
Stimulated gland (TSH or TSH receptor antibodies): tall columnar cells and scant colloid with a scalloped edge where it is being taken back into the cells.
Graves disease shows this active pattern, often with papillary infoldings and patchy lymphocytes.
Parafollicular C cells: pale cells between or beside the follicles that secrete calcitonin.
notes.why: Follicular cell height and colloid volume show how hard TSH, or a stimulating antibody acting at the TSH receptor, is driving the gland. TSH stimulates both endocytosis of colloid for hormone release and follicular cell growth, so an active gland has tall cells and little colloid with a scalloped edge. A quiet gland stores its hormone as thyroglobulin, so its follicles are large, full of colloid, and lined by flat cells.

points: Zona glomerulosa: thin outer layer of cells in rounded clusters; makes aldosterone.
Zona fasciculata: thickest layer, long straight cords of pale, lipid-filled cells (spongiocytes); makes cortisol.
Zona reticularis: innermost cortex, a branching network of smaller, darker cells; makes adrenal androgens (DHEA).
Medulla: chromaffin cells that secrete catecholamines, mostly epinephrine, under sympathetic preganglionic control.
notes.why: Each cortical zone makes a different steroid because each expresses a different set of enzymes. Only the glomerulosa has aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) and it lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it makes mineralocorticoid under angiotensin II and potassium control, while the fasciculata and reticularis express 17-alpha-hydroxylase and respond to ACTH. The pale, foamy look of the fasciculata comes from lipid droplets of stored cholesterol ester, the raw material for steroid synthesis.

points: Acidophils (pink): somatotrophs (GH) and lactotrophs (prolactin).
Basophils (blue or purple): gonadotrophs (FSH, LH), corticotrophs (ACTH), thyrotrophs (TSH).
Chromophobes: pale cells with few granules, many of them degranulated hormone cells.
Posterior pituitary has no hormone-making cells: it holds unmyelinated axons from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, glial pituicytes, and capillaries.
Herring bodies are swellings of those axon terminals packed with granules of ADH or oxytocin.
notes.why: Staining reflects the chemistry of the stored hormone: the simple protein hormones GH and prolactin take up acid dyes, while the glycoprotein hormones (FSH, LH, TSH) and ACTH, which comes from the glycosylated precursor POMC, take up basic and PAS stains. The posterior lobe has no secretory cells because it is a store of hypothalamic axons; ADH and oxytocin are made in the cell bodies, carried down bound to neurophysin, and released at the terminals. This is why removing only the posterior lobe often causes temporary diabetes insipidus, since cut axons higher in the stalk can still release ADH, while destroying the hypothalamic nuclei causes lasting deficiency.

points: Parathyroid chief cells: small, numerous cells that secrete PTH.
Oxyphil cells: larger cells with pink, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm that appear around puberty and increase with age; their function is unclear.
Islets of Langerhans: pale clusters of cells scattered among the darker exocrine acini.
Beta cells (insulin) are the most numerous; alpha cells make glucagon; delta cells make somatostatin.
notes.why: Chief cells sense ionized calcium directly through the calcium-sensing receptor and need no pituitary trophic hormone, so their secretion tracks serum calcium minute to minute. Islet hormones also act on neighboring islet cells (paracrine control): insulin and somatostatin restrain glucagon release, and somatostatin dampens insulin release. Because beta cells make up most of the islet, the islets left in long-standing type 1 diabetes are small and made mostly of alpha and delta cells.

points: Neural crest: adrenal chromaffin cells and thyroid C cells.
Endoderm: thyroid follicular cells, parathyroids, and islets.
Ectoderm: adenohypophysis (oral ectoderm) and neurohypophysis (neuroectoderm). Mesoderm: adrenal cortex.
Neuroendocrine cells store hormones in dense-core secretory granules that contain chromogranin and express synaptophysin.
Immunostains for chromogranin and synaptophysin mark neuroendocrine tumors such as pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, carcinoid tumors, and islet cell tumors.
notes.why: Neuroendocrine cells, whether they come from neural crest or endoderm, share a neuron-like secretory program and store amine or peptide hormones in dense-core granules. Chromogranin A is a protein of the granule matrix and synaptophysin is a protein of the vesicle membrane, so staining for them marks a tumor as neuroendocrine no matter which hormone it makes. Origin also predicts tumor syndromes: in MEN2, an activating RET mutation causes medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma, both tumors of neural crest derived cells.

tricks.label: Busy cells stand tall
tricks.text: A working thyroid cell grows tall and eats its colloid, so tall cells with scalloped colloid mean stimulation, and flat cells with a lake of colloid mean rest.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma comes from C cells, makes calcitonin, and stains for chromogranin.
Pheochromocytoma cells are chromaffin cells and stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin.
Excess ACTH enlarges the fasciculata and reticularis of both adrenals; a cortisol-making adrenal tumor suppresses ACTH, so the other adrenal shrinks.
The posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin made by hypothalamic neurons; it makes no hormone of its own.
Beta cells are the most numerous islet cells and are the cells destroyed in type 1 diabetes.
pitfalls: Basophils include ACTH cells, and acidophils include GH and prolactin cells; do not reverse them.
Parathyroid chief cells make PTH; oxyphil cells are a separate, larger pink cell type.
Herring bodies are axon terminal swellings; pituicytes are glial support cells, not secretory cells.
Adrenal medulla and C cells are neural crest, while thyroid follicular cells and parathyroids are endoderm.

summary: Where the endocrine glands sit in the body and what lies next to them. Exam questions use these neighbors to predict what goes wrong in surgery or with a growing tumor: hoarseness after thyroidectomy, hypocalcemia from removed parathyroids, and visual field loss from a pituitary mass.

points: Two lobes lie beside the larynx and trachea, joined by an isthmus over the second and third tracheal rings.
The gland is enclosed in the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia, which binds it to the larynx and trachea.
Because of that attachment, the thyroid and any mass within it rise with the larynx when the patient swallows.
notes.why: The pretracheal fascia binds the thyroid to the larynx and trachea, so the gland is carried upward with the larynx during swallowing. That makes swallowing a bedside test: a neck mass that rises with swallowing is in or attached to the thyroid, while a thyroglossal duct cyst also rises with tongue protrusion because of its tongue-base attachment. The same fascial attachment explains why a large goiter can compress or push aside the trachea, and the isthmus lying over the upper tracheal rings matters for tracheostomy.

points: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs up in the groove between the trachea and esophagus, close to the inferior thyroid artery near the lower pole.
It supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid.
Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury: hoarse, weak voice from a paralyzed vocal fold.
Bilateral injury: both folds can rest near the midline, causing stridor and airway obstruction.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery to the cricothyroid muscle.
Injury to the external branch causes a weak, monotone voice with loss of high pitch, because the cricothyroid tenses the vocal fold.
notes.why: The two nerves split laryngeal function: the recurrent laryngeal nerve opens and closes the glottis through every intrinsic muscle except the cricothyroid, while the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve sets vocal fold tension through the cricothyroid. Each nerve lies close to a thyroid artery, the recurrent near the inferior thyroid artery and the external branch beside the superior thyroid artery, so ligating those vessels in thyroidectomy is where injury happens. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds, so bilateral recurrent nerve injury leaves the folds unable to open and the airway narrowed.

points: Usually four small glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, outside the thyroid capsule.
The superior glands are fairly constant, near the level of the cricoid cartilage.
The inferior glands vary most, from the lower thyroid poles down into the thymus or mediastinum, because of their long embryonic migration.
Some people have more than four glands, so surgeons must find each one to spare them in thyroidectomy or to remove an adenoma.
notes.why: Position follows embryology: the superior glands from the fourth pouch move only a short distance and stay near the level of the cricoid cartilage, while the inferior glands from the third pouch migrate with the thymus and can stop anywhere along that path. This is why a parathyroid adenoma missed at surgery is often ectopic in the thymus or anterior mediastinum, and why preoperative localization imaging such as a sestamibi scan is used.

points: Sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica in the sphenoid bone.
The diaphragma sellae, a dural fold, roofs the fossa and lets the stalk pass through.
Above: the optic chiasm, where nasal retinal fibers cross.
Lateral: the cavernous sinuses, containing the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI.
Below: the sphenoid sinus, the route for transsphenoidal surgery.
A tumor growing upward presses on the crossing fibers and causes bitemporal hemianopia; growth sideways can cause cranial nerve palsies such as double vision.
notes.why: The sella holds the pituitary in a small bony box, so a growing adenoma takes the path of least resistance: upward through the diaphragma sellae or sideways into the cavernous sinus. Upward growth compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibers at the chiasm, which carry the temporal visual fields, so both temporal fields are lost. Sideways growth affects cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI; the abducens nerve runs within the sinus next to the internal carotid artery, while the others run in its lateral wall.

points: Retroperitoneal, on the superomedial poles of the kidneys, enclosed in renal fascia with a fat layer separating them from the kidney.
Right adrenal: pyramidal, lying behind the inferior vena cava and touching the bare area of the liver.
Left adrenal: crescent-shaped, along the medial border of the left kidney above the hilum, behind the stomach and pancreas.
notes.why: The difference between the two adrenals follows the structures beside them. The right gland sits behind the inferior vena cava, so its very short vein enters the cava directly, which makes the right side harder to remove and a source of bleeding at surgery. A fascial septum inside the renal fascia separates each adrenal from its kidney, so the adrenal stays in place when the kidney is displaced or removed.

summary: How blood reaches and leaves the thyroid, parathyroids, pituitary, adrenals, and islets. The exam uses blood supply to explain why the anterior pituitary infarcts after severe hemorrhage, why calcium falls after thyroid surgery, why the medulla makes epinephrine, and why the liver sees insulin first.

points: Superior thyroid artery: usually the first branch of the external carotid, enters the upper pole.
Inferior thyroid artery: from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian, enters the lower posterior gland.
Thyroid ima artery: present in a minority of people (about 10%), rising from the brachiocephalic trunk or aortic arch to the isthmus; it can bleed in a tracheostomy.
Veins: superior and middle thyroid veins drain to the internal jugular; inferior thyroid veins drain to the brachiocephalic veins.
notes.why: The thyroid has a very high blood flow for its size, supplied by paired superior and inferior arteries that anastomose freely, so tying one artery does not leave the gland without blood. The superior artery comes from the external carotid and the inferior from the subclavian through the thyrocervical trunk. The inferior thyroid veins form a plexus in front of the trachea and drain to the brachiocephalic veins, so they, along with a thyroid ima artery when present, are the bleeding risks in a low midline tracheostomy.

points: Both pairs get their blood mainly from branches of the inferior thyroid artery.
Tying the inferior thyroid artery close to the gland, or removing parathyroid tissue, can leave the parathyroids without PTH output.
Result: hypocalcemia within a day or two of thyroidectomy, with perioral tingling, muscle cramps, and Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
notes.why: Parathyroid glands are tiny and depend on fine end branches, mostly from the inferior thyroid artery, so cutting off their blood is as harmful as removing them. Without PTH, less calcium is released from bone, less is reabsorbed in the distal tubule, and less calcitriol is made, so ionized calcium falls over the first one to two days after surgery. Low ionized calcium lowers the firing threshold of nerve and muscle membranes, producing perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, and the Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

points: Superior hypophyseal arteries (from the internal carotid) form a capillary plexus in the median eminence.
Hypothalamic releasing hormones enter this plexus and travel down the stalk in hypophyseal portal veins.
The portal veins open into a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary.
The anterior lobe gets most of its blood through this low-pressure portal route, with little direct arterial supply.
The posterior lobe gets direct arterial blood from the inferior hypophyseal arteries.
Sheehan syndrome: the pituitary enlarges in pregnancy, and severe postpartum hemorrhage with hypotension infarcts the anterior lobe; failure to lactate is often the first sign.
notes.why: The portal arrangement lets tiny amounts of hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary at high concentration without being diluted in the systemic blood. Because the anterior lobe depends mainly on this low-pressure portal flow, it is vulnerable to ischemia when blood pressure falls, especially when lactotroph hyperplasia has enlarged it in pregnancy. The posterior lobe has its own arterial supply, so Sheehan syndrome usually spares it and the losses are prolactin, gonadotropins, ACTH, TSH, and GH.

points: Three arteries on each side: superior suprarenal (from the inferior phrenic), middle suprarenal (from the aorta), inferior suprarenal (from the renal artery).
One central vein on each side: the right drains straight into the inferior vena cava, the left into the left renal vein.
Blood flows from the capsule through cortical sinusoids into the medulla, carrying high cortisol levels.
Cortisol induces PNMT in chromaffin cells, which converts norepinephrine to epinephrine; this is why the medulla mainly makes epinephrine.
notes.why: Most adrenal blood flows from the outside in: from the capsule through the cortex in sinusoids and then into the medulla, so chromaffin cells are bathed in cortisol at levels far above those in the general circulation. That local cortisol induces PNMT, the enzyme that methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine, which links the cortex to the medulla's main product. The venous anatomy matters in adrenal vein sampling for primary aldosteronism: the short right vein entering the inferior vena cava is hard to catheterize, while the left vein joins the left renal vein.

points: Pancreatic veins drain to the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, then to the hepatic portal vein.
The liver, the main target of both insulin and glucagon, receives them at much higher concentration than the rest of the body.
The liver removes about half of the insulin in portal blood on its first pass.
C-peptide is released in equal amounts with insulin but is not cleared by the liver much, so it tracks the pancreas's own insulin output better than insulin does.
Injected insulin enters the systemic circulation first, which reverses the normal portal-to-peripheral gradient.
notes.why: Islet hormones drain into the portal vein, so the liver sees insulin and glucagon at concentrations several times higher than other tissues, which suits its role as the main glucose buffer. The liver extracts insulin on first pass but clears little C-peptide, so C-peptide reflects the body's own insulin secretion; this separates an insulinoma (high insulin and high C-peptide) from injected insulin (high insulin and low C-peptide). Injected insulin reaches muscle and fat first, reversing the normal gradient in which the liver gets the highest dose.

summary: How the hypothalamus and endocrine glands control each other and what signals switch each hormone on or off. The exam tests the hypothalamic hormones and pituitary stalk injury, ADH control, calcium and PTH, aldosterone, the steps of insulin release, and the hormones that defend blood glucose.

points: TRH raises TSH (and prolactin); CRH raises ACTH; pulsatile GnRH raises LH and FSH; GHRH raises GH.
Somatostatin lowers GH and TSH; dopamine lowers prolactin.
Prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone held down mainly by inhibition.
Pituitary stalk section cuts the portal flow: prolactin rises while GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, and FSH fall.
Stalk section also stops ADH from reaching the posterior lobe, so central diabetes insipidus can develop.
notes.why: Most anterior pituitary hormones depend on stimulatory releasing hormones, so cutting off portal blood removes that drive and their levels fall. Prolactin is the exception because tonic dopamine acting on D2 receptors is its main control, so losing portal dopamine frees the lactotrophs and prolactin rises. GnRH must arrive in pulses: continuous GnRH downregulates its receptor on gonadotrophs and suppresses LH and FSH, which is the basis for using long-acting GnRH agonists to shut down sex steroid production.

points: Made mainly in the supraoptic (and paraventricular) nuclei and released from the posterior pituitary.
Main trigger: a rise in plasma osmolality (normal about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg) sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors; a change of about 1% is enough.
Second trigger: a fall in blood volume or pressure sensed by baroreceptors, which needs a larger change but gives a strong response.
ADH binds V2 receptors (Gs, cAMP) on collecting duct principal cells, which insert aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane.
Water then moves out of the duct into the hypertonic medulla, and urine becomes concentrated.
notes.why: Osmoreceptor neurons near the anterior wall of the third ventricle shrink when plasma osmolality rises and signal the supraoptic and paraventricular neurons to release ADH and to trigger thirst. ADH at V2 receptors raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, which moves aquaporin-2 vesicles into the luminal membrane of principal cells, so water follows the medullary gradient out of the duct. A large fall in blood volume can override osmotic control, which is why patients with hypovolemia keep retaining water and become hyponatremic.

points: Normal total serum calcium is about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL; only the ionized fraction is active and regulated.
The calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid chief cells lowers PTH release when ionized calcium rises.
Bone: PTH acts on osteoblasts to raise RANKL, which activates osteoclasts and releases calcium and phosphate.
Distal tubule: PTH increases calcium reabsorption.
Proximal tubule: PTH blocks phosphate reabsorption, causing phosphate loss in urine.
Proximal tubule: PTH stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase, raising calcitriol, which increases gut calcium and phosphate absorption.
Net effect of PTH: serum calcium up, serum phosphate down. Calcitonin from C cells inhibits osteoclasts and lowers calcium, a minor effect in adults.
notes.why: The calcium-sensing receptor is a G protein coupled receptor whose activation by calcium suppresses PTH release, giving a steep inverse curve in which small drops in ionized calcium cause large rises in PTH. PTH defends calcium in three places: fast calcium retention in the kidney, bone release through osteoblast RANKL that indirectly activates osteoclasts, and slower gut absorption through calcitriol. Phosphate wasting is built in because PTH reduces sodium-phosphate cotransport in the proximal tubule; without it, phosphate released from bone would bind calcium and blunt the rise in free calcium.

points: Main stimuli: angiotensin II and high serum potassium; ACTH has a small, short-lived effect.
Principal cells: more ENaC sodium channels on the luminal side and more Na/K-ATPase on the blood side, so more sodium is reabsorbed.
The sodium movement makes the lumen negative and drives potassium secretion through luminal potassium channels.
Alpha intercalated cells: more H+ secretion through H+-ATPase.
So aldosterone excess causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
notes.why: Aldosterone enters principal cells and binds the mineralocorticoid receptor, which acts as a transcription factor to increase ENaC and Na/K-ATPase activity. Sodium reabsorbed through ENaC without an accompanying anion leaves the lumen electrically negative, which drives potassium out through ROMK channels and favors H+ secretion by intercalated cells. High potassium stimulates aldosterone directly by depolarizing glomerulosa cells, which gives the body a potassium feedback loop that works apart from blood volume.

points: Glucose enters the beta cell by GLUT2 and is trapped by glucokinase, the beta cell's glucose sensor.
Glucose metabolism raises ATP, which closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels.
The cell depolarizes, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and calcium influx triggers insulin exocytosis.
Oral glucose releases more insulin than the same glucose level given IV because gut incretins add to the signal.
Incretins: GLP-1 from intestinal L cells and GIP from duodenal and jejunal K cells raise beta cell cAMP and amplify glucose-driven release.
notes.why: The beta cell works as a fuel sensor: glucokinase has a high Km and is not inhibited by its product, so glycolytic flux and ATP production rise in step with blood glucose across the normal range. Closing the ATP-sensitive potassium channel couples metabolism to membrane voltage, and sulfonylureas trigger the same step by binding its SUR1 subunit. Incretins amplify secretion only when glucose is elevated, which is why GLP-1 based drugs rarely cause hypoglycemia when used alone.

points: As glucose falls, insulin secretion drops first, then glucagon and epinephrine rise.
Glucagon acts within minutes on the liver: glycogen breakdown, then gluconeogenesis.
Epinephrine acts within minutes: liver glycogen breakdown, lipolysis, suppression of insulin release, and the warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tremor, sweating, palpitations).
Cortisol and GH act over hours: cortisol supplies gluconeogenic substrate and enzymes; GH raises lipolysis and reduces glucose uptake.
Long-standing type 1 diabetes often loses the glucagon response, so epinephrine becomes the main defense.
notes.why: Defenses against hypoglycemia switch on at successively lower glucose thresholds: insulin falls first, then glucagon and epinephrine rise, then cortisol and GH, and cognitive impairment from brain glucose lack appears last. Glucagon and epinephrine raise glucose within minutes through cAMP-driven hepatic glycogenolysis, while cortisol and GH work by changing gene expression and so need hours. In long-standing type 1 diabetes the glucagon response is lost, and repeated hypoglycemia blunts the epinephrine response as well, producing hypoglycemia unawareness.

summary: How hormones reach their targets and act on them, and how feedback loops let you locate a disorder from a pair of lab values. The exam asks which second messenger a hormone uses, why total and free hormone levels can disagree, what thyroid hormone, GH, and cortisol do, and why high prolactin shuts down the gonads.

points: Gs and cAMP: ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, PTH, glucagon (also CRH, GHRH, calcitonin, ADH at V2).
Gq and IP3 with calcium: GnRH, TRH, oxytocin (also ADH at V1, angiotensin II).
Intrinsic tyrosine kinase: insulin and IGF-1.
JAK/STAT (receptor-associated tyrosine kinase): GH and prolactin.
Intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors: steroid hormones, thyroid hormone, and calcitriol; their effects take hours.
notes.why: The receptor class follows the hormone's chemistry. Water-soluble peptide hormones cannot cross the membrane, so they act through surface receptors and second messengers within seconds to minutes; steroids and calcitriol diffuse into the cell, and thyroid hormone is carried in by membrane transporters, and all of these bind intracellular receptors that change gene transcription over hours. Gs raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, while Gq activates phospholipase C, whose products IP3 and DAG release stored calcium and activate protein kinase C. The insulin receptor phosphorylates IRS proteins and signals through PI3K-Akt, while GH and prolactin receptors lack their own kinase and recruit JAK2.

points: Thyroid hormone travels mostly bound to thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG); only a tiny free fraction (well under 1%) is active.
Cortisol travels mostly bound to cortisol-binding globulin (CBG); roughly 5 to 10% is free.
Only free hormone enters cells, acts on receptors, and feeds back on the pituitary.
Estrogen (pregnancy, oral contraceptives) raises TBG: total T4 rises, but free T4 and TSH stay normal and the patient is euthyroid.
Low TBG (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure, androgens) lowers total T4 with normal free T4.
notes.why: Binding proteins act as a circulating reservoir and slow hormone clearance, but only the free fraction is sensed by the hypothalamus and pituitary. When binding protein rises, more hormone is bound, free hormone dips briefly, and TSH rises until the larger bound pool fills; free hormone and TSH then settle back to normal at a higher total level. The reverse happens when binding protein falls, so total T4 alone can mislead, and free T4 with TSH is the correct way to judge thyroid status.

points: Target hormone and trophic hormone move in opposite directions: the problem is in the target gland (primary).
Both move in the same direction: the problem is above the gland, in the pituitary or hypothalamus.
Low free T4 with high TSH: primary hypothyroidism.
High cortisol with low ACTH: adrenal tumor or steroid medication; high cortisol with high ACTH: pituitary adenoma or ectopic ACTH.
Low cortisol with high ACTH: primary adrenal insufficiency; low with low: pituitary or hypothalamic disease.
A releasing-hormone stimulation test separates pituitary failure (no response) from hypothalamic failure (pituitary still responds).
notes.why: Negative feedback ties each target hormone to its trophic hormone, so the direction of the pair locates the lesion. A failing or autonomous target gland moves its own hormone first and the intact pituitary responds in the opposite direction, while a pituitary or hypothalamic problem changes the trophic hormone first and the target hormone follows in the same direction. High cortisol with high ACTH needs one more step, the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, because a pituitary adenoma still partly suppresses while an ectopic ACTH source usually does not.

points: The thyroid secretes mostly T4; deiodinases in tissues remove one iodine to make T3, the more active form.
Raises basal metabolic rate, oxygen use, and heat production, partly by increasing Na/K-ATPase.
Increases beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart: higher heart rate, contractility, and cardiac output.
Needed for bone growth (with GH) and for brain maturation; lack in infancy causes intellectual disability and short stature.
notes.why: T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors on thyroid response elements and changes gene transcription, so its effects build over days. More Na/K-ATPase and other energy-consuming processes raise ATP turnover, oxygen use, and heat output, which explains heat intolerance and weight loss in hyperthyroidism. In the heart, more beta-1 receptors and more calcium-handling and contractile proteins explain tachycardia and palpitations, and why beta blockers relieve many symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.

points: GH is released in pulses, mostly in deep sleep, and rises with exercise, fasting, and hypoglycemia.
GHRH stimulates release; somatostatin and IGF-1 feedback suppress it; a glucose load suppresses it in healthy people.
Direct GH actions: lipolysis and insulin antagonism, which raise blood glucose.
Indirect actions through IGF-1 from the liver: linear bone growth at the growth plates and protein synthesis.
notes.why: GH acts at two levels: direct metabolic effects through its own receptor, and growth effects mainly through IGF-1 made in the liver and locally in tissues. The direct effects oppose insulin, so GH excess in acromegaly commonly causes glucose intolerance or diabetes. In a healthy person a glucose load suppresses GH, but an autonomous adenoma does not suppress, which is why the oral glucose suppression test confirms acromegaly; IGF-1 is the screening test because it stays steady through the day while GH pulses.

points: Cortisol raises glucose by gluconeogenesis, and supplies substrate by protein breakdown and lipolysis.
Cortisol is anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive, and it reduces collagen synthesis, so skin thins and wounds heal slowly.
Cortisol is permissive for catecholamine vasoconstriction, which helps maintain blood pressure.
ACTH and cortisol peak in the early morning around waking and are lowest near midnight.
Prolactin is held down by tonic dopamine from the hypothalamus and stimulated by TRH.
High prolactin suppresses GnRH, so LH and FSH fall: amenorrhea and infertility in women, low libido and erectile dysfunction in men.
notes.why: Cortisol acts through the glucocorticoid receptor to change gene expression, so its effects are broad: it induces gluconeogenic enzymes such as PEPCK, breaks down muscle protein for substrate, and suppresses inflammatory genes including those for cytokines and prostaglandin synthesis. Its permissive role includes keeping vascular smooth muscle responsive to catecholamines, which is why cortisol deficiency causes hypotension that responds poorly to pressors. Prolactin excess causes hypogonadism by suppressing hypothalamic GnRH pulses, and primary hypothyroidism can raise prolactin because high TRH stimulates lactotrophs.

summary: The biochemistry behind insulin, glucagon, ketones, and the nutrients the endocrine system depends on: iodine, selenium, vitamin D, and magnesium. It also covers leptin and ghrelin in appetite control. The exam links each nutrient or pathway step to the disease that follows when it fails.

points: Insulin moves GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
Liver and muscle: activates glycogen synthase, so glucose is stored as glycogen.
Speeds glycolysis and, in the liver, turns extra glucose into fatty acids (lipogenesis through acetyl-CoA carboxylase).
Adipose: raises lipoprotein lipase to take up triglyceride and blocks hormone-sensitive lipase.
Increases protein synthesis and drives potassium into cells.
notes.why: Insulin acts through its receptor tyrosine kinase and the PI3K-Akt pathway, and it lowers cAMP by activating phosphodiesterase, so it reverses the phosphorylations made by glucagon and epinephrine. Dephosphorylation activates glycogen synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase and inactivates glycogen phosphorylase and hormone-sensitive lipase, so fuel is stored instead of released. Insulin also stimulates Na/K-ATPase, which is why insulin given with glucose is used to shift potassium into cells in hyperkalemia.

points: Glucagon acts mainly on the liver through cAMP and protein kinase A; muscle has few glucagon receptors.
Activates glycogen phosphorylase for glycogenolysis; liver glycogen lasts about a day of fasting.
Lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, turning off glycolysis and turning on gluconeogenesis.
Lowers malonyl-CoA, which releases CPT-1, so fatty acids enter mitochondria for oxidation and ketogenesis.
notes.why: Glucagon raises cAMP in hepatocytes, and protein kinase A phosphorylates key enzymes to reverse the fed pattern: phosphorylase becomes active and glycogen synthase becomes inactive. PKA also phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme so it breaks down fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which slows PFK-1 and releases fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, so carbon flows toward glucose. Phosphorylated acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes less malonyl-CoA, which removes the brake on CPT-1 so fatty acids enter mitochondria for beta-oxidation and ketone production.

points: No insulin plus high glucagon: hormone-sensitive lipase runs freely and floods the liver with fatty acids.
Beta-oxidation makes more acetyl-CoA than the TCA cycle can use, since oxaloacetate is pulled into gluconeogenesis.
The liver converts the excess acetyl-CoA via HMG-CoA to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.
These ketoacids release H+, lower bicarbonate, and raise the anion gap (normal about 8 to 12 mEq/L).
Acetone forms from acetoacetate and gives a fruity breath odor; deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing compensates.
The liver makes ketones but cannot use them; brain, heart, and muscle can.
notes.why: Insulin deficiency with glucagon excess turns on lipolysis and hepatic fatty acid oxidation at the same time. Oxaloacetate is pulled into gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-CoA cannot enter the TCA cycle and is channeled into ketone bodies; the liver cannot use them because it lacks the enzyme that activates acetoacetate (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase). Ketoacids consume bicarbonate and leave unmeasured anions, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, while glucose-driven osmotic diuresis causes dehydration and total body potassium loss even when serum potassium is normal or high.

points: Iodide enters follicular cells by the sodium-iodide symporter and is attached to thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase.
Iodine deficiency lowers T4 and T3, so TSH rises and drives follicular cell growth: goiter.
Severe deficiency in pregnancy causes congenital hypothyroidism with intellectual disability.
The deiodinases that convert T4 to T3 contain selenium (as selenocysteine).
Selenium is also in glutathione peroxidase, which protects the thyroid from the peroxide it uses to make hormone.
notes.why: Thyroid peroxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize iodide so it can be attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, and it then couples the iodotyrosines into T4 and T3. When iodine is scarce, hormone output falls, loss of negative feedback raises TSH, and TSH drives follicular cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia, producing a goiter as the gland works to trap more iodide. Selenium matters at two points: deiodinases need selenocysteine to make T3 from T4, and glutathione peroxidase protects follicular cells from the peroxide generated during hormone synthesis.

points: UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol); diet adds D2 and D3.
Liver 25-hydroxylase makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form and the best measure of vitamin D status.
Kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase (proximal tubule) makes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), the active form; PTH and low phosphate stimulate it.
Deficiency: less calcium absorbed, PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism), phosphate is lost in urine, and bone mineralizes poorly.
Children get rickets (bowed legs, rachitic rosary, wide growth plates); adults get osteomalacia (bone pain, pseudofractures).
Typical labs: low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, high PTH, high alkaline phosphatase, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
notes.why: Vitamin D is a prohormone that needs two hydroxylations, first in the liver and then in the kidney, and only the kidney step is tightly regulated. 25-hydroxyvitamin D has a long half-life and reflects body stores, while calcitriol can stay normal or even rise early in deficiency because the high PTH stimulates its production. Poor calcium absorption triggers secondary hyperparathyroidism, which holds serum calcium near normal at the cost of phosphate wasting; the low calcium-phosphate product leaves osteoid unmineralized, the lesion of rickets and osteomalacia.

points: Severe low magnesium blocks PTH release and makes bone and kidney resistant to PTH.
The result is hypocalcemia that will not correct with calcium alone until magnesium is replaced.
Common causes: alcohol use disorder, chronic diarrhea, poor intake, long-term proton pump inhibitor use, and diuretics.
notes.why: Both PTH secretion and PTH action on bone and kidney need adequate magnesium. Mild magnesium deficiency can stimulate PTH much as low calcium does, but severe depletion blocks PTH release and causes end-organ resistance, so serum calcium stays low despite calcium replacement. Magnesium deficiency also releases ROMK channels in the kidney from their normal magnesium block, so hypokalemia often coexists and is also hard to correct until magnesium is restored.

points: Leptin comes from adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and signals satiety to the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
Leptin stimulates POMC neurons (alpha-MSH acting on MC4R) and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons, lowering intake.
Ghrelin comes from the stomach, rises before meals, and stimulates NPY/AgRP neurons to cause hunger.
Common obesity has high leptin with leptin resistance; true leptin deficiency is rare.
Visceral fat releases fatty acids into the portal vein and inflammatory cytokines, and makes less adiponectin, which promotes insulin resistance.
notes.why: Leptin and ghrelin act on opposing neuron groups in the arcuate nucleus: POMC neurons release alpha-MSH, which acts on MC4R to reduce intake and raise energy expenditure, while NPY/AgRP neurons drive feeding and AgRP blocks MC4R. In common obesity, signaling downstream of the leptin receptor is impaired, so high leptin no longer suppresses appetite. Visceral fat delivers free fatty acids straight to the liver through the portal vein and secretes TNF-alpha and IL-6 while making less adiponectin, and together these impair insulin signaling in liver and muscle.

tricks.label: Insulin stores, glucagon spends
tricks.text: Every pathway that builds storage (glycogen, fat, protein) is insulin's; every pathway that releases fuel (glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenesis, ketones) is glucagon's.

tricks.label: Fix magnesium first
tricks.text: If calcium stays low after calcium is given, check magnesium. Without it the parathyroids cannot release PTH and tissues cannot respond to it.

tricks.label: Ghrelin growls
tricks.text: Ghrelin is the hunger hormone from the stomach; leptin is the fat-made signal that you have eaten enough.

highYield: DKA: high glucose, ketones, low bicarbonate, and a raised anion gap.
The urine nitroprusside test detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, the main ketone in DKA.
Iodine deficiency is the most common cause of goiter worldwide.
25-hydroxyvitamin D measures vitamin D stores; calcitriol does not, since PTH keeps it up until late.
Chronic kidney disease lowers 1-alpha-hydroxylase, causing low calcitriol and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Hypocalcemia that does not respond to calcium points to hypomagnesemia.
Most people with obesity have high leptin levels, reflecting resistance to its signal.
pitfalls: Glucagon has little effect on skeletal muscle; epinephrine drives muscle glycogen breakdown.
The liver makes ketones but lacks the enzyme to use them, so it never consumes its own product.
Rickets and osteomalacia are the same mineralization defect at different ages; osteoporosis has normal mineralization with less bone.
Selenium helps convert T4 to T3; iodine is the building block of the hormone itself.
